The Last of Isaiah's Prophecies as to Sennacherib's Overthrow.</title> <div sID="gen14938" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Is 33:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">8, 9</reference>, describe the Assyrian spoiler; strong as he is, he shall fall before Jehovah who is stronger (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.2-Isa.6.10">Is 33:2-6, 10</reference>-12). The time is the autumn of 713 B.C.<div eID="gen14938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8916"/><hi type="bold">1. and thou--</hi>that is, though thou wast not spoiled--though thou wast not dealt treacherously with (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.24.16">Is 24:16</reference>), thy spoiling and treachery are therefore without excuse, being unprovoked.<div eID="gen14939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14940" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cease--</hi>When God has let thee do thy worst, in execution of His plans, thine own turn shall come (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">Is 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.2">14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.8">Ha 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Re 13:10</reference>). <div eID="gen14940" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 33 Is 33:1-24 . The Last of Isaiah's Prophecies as to Sennacherib's Overthrow. Is 33:1 , 8, 9 , describe the Assyrian spoiler; strong as he is, he shall fall before Jehovah who is stronger ( Is 33:2-6, 10 -12). The time is the autumn of 713 B.C. 1. and thou-- that is, though thou wast not spoiled--though thou wast not dealt treacherously with (see on Is 24:16 ), thy spoiling and treachery are therefore without excuse, being unprovoked. cease-- When God has let thee do thy worst, in execution of His plans, thine own turn shall come (compare Is 10:12 ; 14:2 ; Ha 2:8 ; Re 13:10 ).

Thine--</hi>the saints'.<div eID="gen14979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">king in ... beauty--</hi>not as now, Hezekiah in sackcloth, oppressed by the enemy, but King Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">Is 32:1</reference>) "in His beauty" (<reference osisRef="Song.5.10">So 5:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.5.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.4.3">Re 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen14980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14981" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">land ... very far off--</hi>rather, "the land in its remotest extent" (no longer pent up as Hezekiah was with the siege); see Margin. Two scribes are seen in every Assyrian bas-relief, writing down the various objects brought to them, the heads of the slain, prisoners, cattle, sheep, &c. receiver-- "weigher," Margin. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8937"/><div sID="gen14998" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8937"/><hi type="bold">23. tacklings--</hi>Continuing the allegory in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.21">Is 33:21</reference>, he compares the enemies' host to a war galley which is deprived of the tacklings or cords by which the mast is sustained and the sail is spread; and which therefore is sure to be wrecked on "the broad river" (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.21">Is 33:21</reference>), and become the prey of Israel.<div eID="gen14998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they--</hi>the tacklings, "hold not firm the base of the mast."<div eID="gen14999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15000" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then--</hi>when the Assyrian host shall have been discomfited. Hezekiah had given Sennacherib three hundred talents of silver, and thirty of gold (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.14-2Kgs.18.16">2Ki 18:14-16</reference>), and had stripped the temple of its gold to give it to him; this treasure was probably part of the prey found in the foe's camp. After the invasion, Hezekiah had so much wealth that he made an improper display of it (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.13-2Kgs.20.15">2Ki 20:13-15</reference>); this wealth, probably, was in part got from the Assyrian.<div eID="gen15000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the lame--</hi>Even the most feeble shall spoil the Assyrian camp (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.35.6">Is 35:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.6">2Sa 5:6</reference>). <div eID="gen15001" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8938"/><div sID="gen15002" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8938"/><hi type="bold">24. sick--</hi>Smith thinks the allusion is to the beginning of the pestilence by which the Assyrians were destroyed, and which, while sparing the righteous, affected some within the city ("sinners in Zion"); it may have been the sickness that visited Hezekiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.1-Isa.38.22">Is 38:1-22</reference>). In the Jerusalem to come there shall be no "sickness," because there will be no "iniquity," it being forgiven (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.3">Psa 103:3</reference>). The latter clause of the verse contains the cause of the former (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.5-Mark.2.9">Mr 2:5-9</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.33"/>

navigation_sections.content_plain: CHAPTER 33 Is 33:1-24 . The Last of Isaiah's Prophecies as to Sennacherib's Overthrow. Is 33:1 , 8, 9 , describe the Assyrian spoiler; strong as he is, he shall fall before Jehovah who is stronger ( Is 33:2-6, 10 -12). The time is the autumn of 713 B.C.
